usage: Existence with 있다 plus subject 이/가 — the default way to announce a meeting on the calendar.
회의에 들어가다 'enter a meeting' is the set phrase; use 에 here, not 에서, because you are moving in.
회의 takes 하다 to become a verb; 회의하다 = the act of meeting, distinct from the event noun.
Bare noun + 시간 forms a time phrase; no particle between 회의 and 시간.
examples: 오늘 회의가 두 개 있어요.
I have two meetings today.
Counts meetings with 개; 회의가 (subject) is what 있다 describes.
회의에서 새 계획을 정했어요.
We decided a new plan in the meeting.
에서 marks the meeting as the place where the action happened — contrast with 에 for entering.
부장님이 회의를 길게 끌어서 다들 지쳤어요.
The manager dragged the meeting out, so everyone got worn out.
Real-office register: 회의를 끌다 'drag a meeting out' is the natural complaint collocation.
nuance: 회의 (漢字 會議, 會 'gather' + 議 'discuss') is a formal, work-style meeting where people gather to discuss and decide something — a board meeting, a team sync, a planning session. The near-synonym learners reach for is 모임, but 모임 is a social get-together (a dinner, a club, friends meeting up) with no agenda, so calling drinks with friends a 회의 sounds robotic; conversely calling a budget review a 모임 sounds too loose. It pairs naturally with 회의를 하다 (hold), 회의에 들어가다 (go into), 회의가 길어지다 (run long). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you are *in* a meeting as a location, so the action takes 회의에서, but you *enter* a meeting with 회의에 들어가다 — and never confuse 회의 with the look-alike 회사 (company) or 회비 (membership fee).

mistakes: Saying 친구하고 회의했어요 for hanging out with friends — 회의 implies a formal agenda; for a casual gathering say 친구하고 모였어요 or use 모임.
Using 회의에 for where talking happens, as in 회의에 이야기했어요 — the location of an action needs 에서: 회의에서 이야기했어요. Reserve 회의에 for 들어가다/참석하다.
Mixing up 회의 with 회사; 회사에 가요 means go to the company/office, while 회의에 가요 means go to the meeting.

usage: to fill out / draw up a document.
서류를 작성하다 is the formal verb for completing a form — more office-appropriate than just 쓰다.
There is a lot of paperwork.
서류 is treated as a mass noun here; 많다 describes the pile, no plural marker needed.
제출하다 'hand in/submit' is the set partner for official forms (applications, reports).
Please give me one copy of the document.
Counter for a set/copy of papers is 부, not 개 or 장.
examples: 이 서류 좀 봐 주세요.
Please take a look at this document.
Everyday polite request; 좀 softens the ask, 봐 주세요 = 'look at it for me'.
부장님께 서류를 드렸어요.
I gave the documents to the manager.
Honorific recipient 께 + humble 드리다 because the boss outranks you.
비자 신청 서류가 하나라도 빠지면 접수가 안 돼요.
If even one visa application document is missing, they won't accept it.
Real-life bureaucracy: 서류가 빠지다 'a document is missing' is the natural collocation.
nuance: 서류 (漢字 書類, 書 'write' + 類 'kind/category') means official paperwork — forms, applications, reports, contracts — the documents you submit, sign, and file at work or a government office. It is not a casual word for any paper; a personal notebook is 공책, a book is 책, and a single loose sheet is 종이 (one sheet = 종이 한 장). 서류 usually behaves as a collective even when grammatically singular, so 서류가 많다 means 'there's a lot of paperwork.' It rides with 작성하다 (fill out), 제출하다 (submit), 처리하다 (process), 빠지다 (be missing). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 to count it — use 부 for a copy/set (서류 한 부) or 장 for individual sheets, and don't translate 'do the documents' as 서류를 하다; you 작성하다 or 처리하다 them.

mistakes: Counting with 개 (서류 한 개) — papers are counted with 장 (sheets) or 부 (a copy/set of a document): 서류 한 부.
Calling a personal book or notebook 서류 — 서류 is strictly official paperwork; a notebook is 공책/노트 and a book is 책.
Saying 서류를 해요 to mean 'I do the paperwork' — there is no 서류하다; use 서류를 작성하다 (fill out) or 서류를 처리하다 (handle).

usage: 보내다 'send' is the core verb; the message takes 을/를 as the object.
Incoming mail is the subject of 오다; 이메일이 왔어요 = 'an email came.'
확인하다 'verify/check' is the standard verb for reading your inbox.
Compound noun; 주소 'address' attaches directly with no particle.
examples: 이메일 주소가 뭐예요?
What is your email address?
Beginner exchange; 뭐예요? asks for the information directly.
동료에게 이메일을 보냈어요.
I sent an email to my coworker.
Human recipient takes 에게 (written/neutral) — to a machine/place you'd use 에.
참고로 아까 보낸 이메일에 자료 첨부했으니까 확인 부탁드려요.
FYI, I attached the file to the email I sent earlier, so please check it.
Workplace email register: 첨부하다 'attach', 확인 부탁드려요 'please check' are the real formulas.
nuance: 이메일 is the everyday loanword (from English 'e-mail') for electronic mail, used freely at work and in daily life; the Sino alternative 전자우편 (電子郵便 'electronic post') exists but sounds stiff and bureaucratic, mostly seen on official forms. Crucially, 이메일 ≠ paper mail: a physical letter is 편지, and the postal-mail system is 우편, so 'I got your letter' about a posted envelope is 편지를 받았어요, not 이메일. It collocates with 보내다 (send), 받다 (receive), 확인하다 (check), 첨부하다 (attach a file), 답장하다 (reply). The English-speaker pitfall is the recipient particle — a person who receives mail takes 에게/한테 (동료에게 이메일을 보내요), and don't drag the English verb 'do' over: you 이메일을 보내다 or 쓰다, never 이메일하다.

The recipient particle: a person who receives mail takes 에게/한테 (동료에게 이메일을 보내요). And don't drag the English verb 'do' over — you 이메일을 보내다 or 쓰다, never 이메일하다.

mistakes: Using 이메일 for a posted paper letter — that is 편지 (a letter) or 우편 (postal mail); 이메일 is only the electronic kind.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 (동료를 이메일 보냈어요) — the person gets 에게/한테 and the email is the object: 동료에게 이메일을 보냈어요.
Saying 이메일했어요 to mean 'I emailed' — Korean doesn't verb it that way; say 이메일을 보냈어요 or 이메일을 썼어요.

usage: 회사 modifies 동료 directly; a frequent full phrase for 'colleague at my company.'
와/과 함께 'together with' is the bookish/neutral pairing; spoken Korean often uses 하고 같이.
돕다 (ㅂ-irregular: 도와요) takes the colleague as object with 을/를.
직장 'workplace' + 동료 is an extremely common fixed pairing, near-synonymous with 회사 동료.
examples: 동료가 참 친절해요.
My coworker is really kind.
Simple description; 참 'truly' adds warmth, 친절해요 describes character.
동료하고 같이 점심을 먹어요.
I eat lunch together with a coworker.
Spoken pairing 하고 같이; the everyday equivalent of 와/과 함께.
새로 온 동료가 일을 빨리 배워서 팀에 큰 도움이 돼요.
The newly arrived coworker learns fast, so it's a big help to the team.
Real-office framing; 도움이 되다 'be of help' is the natural result clause.
nuance: 동료 (漢字 同僚, 同 'same' + 僚 'fellow official/colleague') means a colleague — someone you work alongside, typically at a comparable level, with a neutral, slightly formal tone. The line learners blur is with rank words: a work senior is 선배 (or 상사 for a superior/boss), a junior is 후배, so once status is in play Koreans name the rank rather than say 동료. It is also strictly a *work* word — classmates at school are 친구 or 동급생, never 동료. Natural partners: 회사 동료, 직장 동료, 동료와 협력하다 (cooperate), 동료를 돕다. The English-speaker pitfall: 'colleague' in English can loosely include your boss, but Korean 동료 implies a peer — don't call 부장님 your 동료. Also note 동료 is the person; the human-recipient/companion particle is 하고/와, not 를, when you do something *with* them.

mistakes: Calling school classmates 동료 — that is 친구 (friend) or 동급생/반 친구; 동료 is specifically a work colleague.
Referring to your boss as 동료 — a superior is 상사 or by title (부장님); 동료 implies an equal-level peer.
Saying 동료를 점심 먹어요 for eating with a coworker — the companion takes 하고/와: 동료하고 같이 점심을 먹어요.

usage: 사장 almost always carries 님; the verb takes 시 honorific: 오시다 → 오셨어요.
께 is the honorific replacement for 에게/한테 when the recipient outranks you.
모시다 is the humble verb for serving a superior — far politer than 데리다.
Koreans say 우리 ('our') even for one's own boss/company — a collective-belonging idiom.
examples: 사장님이 지금 안 계세요.
The boss is not here right now.
Honorific existence 계시다 → 계세요; negated for absence.
우리 사장님은 직원들을 정말 아끼세요.
Our boss really cares about the employees.
아끼다 'treasure/care for' + 시 honorific; 우리 for one's own company.
사장님께 직접 보고드려야 하는 사안이라 좀 긴장돼요.
It's a matter I have to report directly to the boss, so I'm a bit nervous.
Real-workplace register; 보고드리다 'humbly report' + 께 to a superior.
nuance: 사장 (漢字 社長, 社 'company' + 長 'chief/head') is the head/president/owner of a company. The crucial register fact: at work you virtually never say bare 사장 to or about your boss — it's 사장님, and the verbs go honorific (오시다, 계시다, 말씀하시다) while your own actions toward them go humble (드리다, 보고드리다, 모시다). Distinguish the rank ladder: 부장 is a department head (mid-level), 과장 a section chief, and 사장 sits at the top, with 회장 (chairman) above only in large groups. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 님 (사장 said to their face sounds blunt to the point of rude) and using plain verbs — 사장님이 왔어요 should be 사장님이 오셨어요. Bare 사장 without 님 mainly appears in neutral writing or when referring to a small-shop owner in the third person.

mistakes: Addressing or referring to your own boss as plain 사장 — attach 님: 사장님. Bare 사장 to their face sounds disrespectful.
Using plain verbs for the boss (사장님이 말했어요) — superiors take honorific 시: 사장님이 말씀하셨어요 (말씀하시다 is the honorific of 말하다).
Saying 사장님에게 for 'to the boss' in polite speech — a superior takes the honorific particle 께: 사장님께.

usage: 받다 'receive' is the core verb; the pay is the object with 을/를.
오르다 (르-irregular: 올라요) 'rise' takes the salary as subject — the happy collocation.
월급 + 날 'day' forms one compound noun: the day salary lands.
밀리다 'be pushed back/owed' is the standard verb when pay doesn't come on time.
examples: 오늘 월급 받았어요.
I got paid today.
Plain everyday line; 월급 받다 'get one's salary' as the natural unit.
매달 이십오일에 월급이 들어와요.
My salary comes in on the 25th every month.
월급이 들어오다 'salary comes in (to the account)' + date with 에.
첫 월급으로 부모님께 내복을 사 드렸어요.
With my first paycheck I bought my parents long underwear.
Cultural set phrase: 첫 월급으로 내복을 사 드리다 is a real Korean first-salary custom; 으로 = means.
nuance: 월급 (漢字 月給, 月 'month' + 給 'pay/give') is pay received on a monthly cycle — the everyday word an ordinary worker uses for their paycheck. Distinguish the pay-period family sharply: 시급 (時給) is an hourly wage, 주급 (週給) weekly, and 연봉 (年俸) is annual salary — the figure you negotiate at hiring and quote when comparing jobs. So 'What's the salary?' for a part-time gig is 시급이 얼마예요?, but for a career offer it's 연봉이 얼마예요?; using 월급 there sounds slightly small-scale. Natural partners: 월급을 받다, 월급이 오르다, 월급이 밀리다 (be owed), 월급날, 월급이 들어오다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'salary' as one word — Korean splits it by period, so don't say 월급 when you mean the annual 연봉, and remember it's 받다 (receive), not 'earn-translated-literally.'

Saying 월급을 벌어요 modeled on 'earn a salary' — the natural verb is 받다: 월급을 받아요. (벌다 fits 돈을 벌다 'make money' generally.)

usage: to go to work / clock in.
출근 + 하다 makes the verb; describes heading to and arriving at the workplace.
to go to work at nine.
Clock time takes 에; states your start hour.
Bare compound; can mean rush hour or your designated start time.
the way to work / one's commute.
출근 + 길 'road' = the journey in to work, as in 출근길에 'on the way to work.'
examples: 저는 보통 여덟 시에 출근해요.
I usually go to work at eight.
보통 'usually' sets a routine; 에 marks the clock time.
오늘은 차가 막혀서 출근이 늦었어요.
Today I was late to work because of traffic.
출근이 늦다 'be late getting to work' + reason with 아서.
내일 새벽같이 출근해야 해서 일찍 자려고요.
I have to get to work at the crack of dawn tomorrow, so I plan to sleep early.
새벽같이 출근하다 'go in at dawn' is a natural intensity collocation; ~려고요 states intention.
nuance: 출근 (漢字 出勤, 出 'go out' + 勤 'attend to duty') is going to / showing up for work — both the leaving-home-for-the-job and the arriving/clocking-in sense. Its exact opposite is 퇴근 (退勤, 'withdraw from duty') = leaving work at day's end; the two are a fixed pair Korean learners must keep straight. Don't confuse 출근 (reporting to your job) with 통근 (通勤, the commute itself) or with 등교 (登校, a student going to school) — a pupil 등교하지 출근하지 않아요. Natural partners: 출근하다, 출근 시간, 출근길, 출근이 늦다, 정시 출근 (on-time arrival). The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 conjugation and particles: it's 출근해요 (not a separate verb 'go-work'), the time takes 에 (아홉 시에 출근해요), and the means of commuting takes (으)로 (지하철로 출근해요), never 'by'-translated-as-에서.

Using 출근 for a student going to school — pupils 등교하다 (登校), not 출근하다; 출근 is only for a job.
Marking the means of commute with 에서 (지하철에서 출근해요) — the vehicle/means takes (으)로: 지하철로 출근해요.

usage: 퇴근 + 하다 makes the verb for finishing the day and heading home.
Sino 후 'after' + 에 marks the time slot; the set phrase for evening plans.
정시 (定時 'set time') + 퇴근 = clocking out exactly on schedule, a coveted thing.
퇴근 + 길 'road' = the commute home, as in 퇴근길에 'on the way home.'
examples: 오늘은 일찍 퇴근하고 싶어요.
Today I want to leave work early.
Desire with ~고 싶다; 일찍 퇴근하다 'leave early' is the everyday wish.
퇴근 후에 동료들하고 한잔하기로 했어요.
We decided to grab a drink with coworkers after work.
퇴근 후에 + 한잔하다 'have a drink' — the classic after-work plan; ~기로 하다 'decide to.'
일이 산더미라 오늘도 칼퇴근은 글렀어요.
Work is piled up, so leaving right on the dot is hopeless today too.
Slang 칼퇴근 'knife-sharp on-time clock-out'; very natural colloquial office talk.
nuance: 퇴근 (漢字 退勤, 退 'withdraw/retreat' + 勤 'duty') means leaving the workplace at the end of the working day — clocking out and heading home. Its hardwired opposite is 출근 (出勤) = going to work in the morning; the pair shares 勤 'duty,' with 出 'out (to)' versus 退 'withdraw (from).' Don't blur 퇴근 (going home after work today) with 퇴사 (退社, quitting the company for good) — 오늘 퇴근해요 means you're heading home, 회사를 퇴사해요 means you're resigning. Natural partners: 퇴근하다, 퇴근 후에, 퇴근길, 정시 퇴근, the slang 칼퇴근 (leaving exactly on time). The English-speaker pitfall: 'leave work' tempts a literal 일을 떠나요, but the single word is 퇴근하다; and the time still takes 에 (여섯 시에 퇴근해요), while 후에 attaches to 퇴근 for 'after work.'

mistakes: Swapping 퇴근 and 출근 — 퇴근 is going home (evening), 출근 is arriving at work (morning); they are opposites.

Translating 'leave work' literally as 일을 떠나다 — Korean uses the one verb 퇴근하다; 일을 떠나다 sounds like abandoning a task.

usage: 가다 'go' takes the leave as object with 을/를; the standard 'take a trip' framing.
내다 'put in/submit' is the office verb for filing for time off — 휴가를 내다 'put in for leave.'
中 'middle of' marks an ongoing state: 휴가 중이에요 'I'm on leave.'
여름 'summer' modifies 휴가 directly — the big annual leave most Koreans take.
examples: 다음 주에 휴가를 가요.
I'm going on vacation next week.
Future-ish plan; 에 marks the time, 가요 the going.
이번에 휴가 내고 제주도에 다녀오려고요.
I'm taking leave this time and planning a trip to Jeju.
휴가(를) 내다 'request leave' (office sense) + ~려고요 intention; 다녀오다 'go and come back.'
눈치 보여서 연차 휴가를 마음 편히 쓰기가 어려워요.
I feel self-conscious, so it's hard to use my annual leave with peace of mind.
Real workplace culture: 연차(휴가)를 쓰다 'use one's annual leave' + 눈치 보이다 'feel watched.'
nuance: 휴가 (漢字 休暇, 休 'rest' + 暇 'leisure/free time') is leave taken from a job — paid annual leave (연차 휴가), summer vacation (여름 휴가), or military/special leave. The boundary learners must guard is against 방학: 방학 is a *school* break (winter/summer holidays for students and teachers), so a worker says 휴가 while a student says 방학 — 회사원은 휴가, 학생은 방학. Also distinguish 휴일 (a single day off / public holiday) from 휴가 (a stretch of personal leave). Natural partners: 휴가를 가다 (go on), 휴가를 내다/쓰다 (take, in the office sense), 휴가 중, 연차 휴가. The English-speaker pitfall is using 휴가 for a school vacation (that's 방학) and reaching only for 가다 — to *request* time off at work you 휴가를 내다 or 휴가를 쓰다, which 'go on vacation' alone doesn't capture.

usage: 주고받다 'give-and-take' is the set verb for the two-way card swap at first meetings.
to hand over a business card.
건네다 'pass/hand to' is more polished than 주다 for offering your card.
Flat cards are counted with 장 (sheets), not 개: 명함 한 장.
to hand out one's cards around.
돌리다 'pass around' = distributing cards to several people, e.g. around a table.
examples: 명함 한 장 주세요.
Please give me one of your cards.
Polite request with counter 장; the everyday way to ask for someone's card.
명함에 직책이 적혀 있어요.
The job title is written on the card.
Location with 에; 적혀 있다 'is written (and remains)' — passive resultative.
처음 만나면 두 손으로 명함을 건네는 게 예의예요.
When you first meet, handing your card with both hands is the polite thing.
Cultural manners: 두 손으로 'with both hands' + 건네다; ~는 게 예의다 'it's etiquette to.'
nuance: 명함 (漢字 名銜, 名 'name' + 銜 'title/rank') is a printed business card carrying your name, company, position, and contacts. In Korean work culture the *exchange* is a small ritual — you offer and receive 두 손으로 (with both hands), read the card a beat before pocketing it, and never write on someone's card in front of them. Don't confuse 명함 with 카드 (a generic card / credit card) or 신분증 (an ID card): 명함 is specifically the work introduction card. Natural partners: 명함을 주고받다, 명함을 건네다, 명함을 돌리다, 명함을 받다, 명함에 (직책이) 적혀 있다. The English-speaker pitfall is the counter — flat printed cards take 장 (명함 한 장), not the all-purpose 개; and the polite verb for offering one is 건네다/드리다, while the whole social act is captured by 주고받다, with no real English one-word equivalent.

usage: Static location of existence takes 에 with 있다: 사무실에 있어요.
An action's location takes 에서: 사무실에서 일해요 — contrast with 에 for mere existence.
to move offices / relocate the office.
옮기다 'move/relocate' takes the office as object; said when the workplace changes location.
분위기 'mood' is a very common partner — 사무실 분위기가 좋다 'the office vibe is good.'
examples: 우리 사무실은 삼 층에 있어요.
Our office is on the third floor.
Floor location with 에; 우리 'our' for one's own workplace.
지금 사무실에서 회의 중이에요.
I'm in a meeting at the office right now.
Action-location 에서 + 중이다 'in the middle of'; natural status update.
사무실이 조용해서 집중이 잘돼요.
The office is quiet, so I can concentrate well.
Reason with 아서; 집중이 잘되다 'concentration goes well' — natural result.
nuance: 사무실 (漢字 事務室, 事 'affair' + 務 'duty/task' + 室 'room') is literally the 'task-duty room' — the physical room or space where desk/clerical work is done. Keep it apart from 회사 (會社), which is the *company* as an organization/employer: you work 사무실에서 (in the office room) but you belong to a 회사 (the firm). Also distinguish 사무실 from 사무소 (an office/agency open to clients, e.g. 부동산 사무소 'real-estate office') and from the casual loan 오피스. Natural partners: 사무실에서 일하다, 사무실에 있다, 사무실을 옮기다, 사무실 분위기. The English-speaker pitfall is the 에 vs 에서 split: use 에 for simply being there (사무실에 있어요) but 에서 for doing something there (사무실에서 일해요) — and don't substitute 사무실 when you mean the company itself; that's 회사.

usage: Title + 님 + honorific 시: 부장님이 부르세요 'the manager is calling you.'
to report to the department head.
Superior recipient takes 께; 보고하다 'report' often becomes humble 보고드리다.
Surname + title + 님 is the standard way to address/refer to a ranked superior.
Existence of a superior uses honorific 계시다: 부장님이 계세요.
examples: 부장님이 지금 회의 중이세요.
The department head is in a meeting right now.
Honorific 중이시다; 시 attaches even to the status copula for a superior.
이 서류 부장님께 갖다 드리세요.
Please take this document to the department head.
께 (to a superior) + humble 드리다 + 갖다 드리다 'take and give'; 으세요 command.
부장님이 결재해 주셔야 다음 단계로 넘어갈 수 있어요.
We can move to the next step only once the manager signs off.
Workplace process: 결재하다 'approve/sign off' + 주시다 honorific benefactive; ~어야 'only if.'
nuance: 부장 (漢字 部長, 部 'department/division' + 長 'chief/head') is a department head — a senior manager who runs a 부서 (department), ranking above 과장 (section chief) and 대리, and below executives and the 사장 (company president). Like all Korean rank titles it functions as an honorific address: you say 부장님 (with 님), and you can prefix a surname — 김 부장님. The whole speech frame goes honorific around them (부르시다, 계시다, 결재해 주시다) while your own actions toward them turn humble (보고드리다, 갖다 드리다). Don't confuse the title-as-address with a name — Koreans routinely call the person 부장님 rather than by given name at work. The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 사장: dropping 님 (bare 부장 to their face is rude), using plain verbs instead of honorific 시, and marking the recipient with 에게 instead of the honorific 께.

Marking 'to the manager' with 에게/한테 (부장님에게 보고했어요) — a superior takes 께: 부장님께 보고드렸어요.
